dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Welcome to Student Kitchen — the podcast for university students who want to eat well on a budget. Today we're learning to make manti — the classic Kazakh steamed dumpling. Our guest is Rustam Seilov from WKU. Rustam, how many people does your recipe serve?

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: About eight to ten people. You can make a lot at once and freeze the leftovers.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Perfect. Let's start with the dough. How much flour do you need?

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: About 500 grams — roughly four cups. Not too much or the dough gets too heavy.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: About 200ml of warm water. Add it little by little — you don't want too much at once or it gets sticky.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: How many eggs go into the dough?

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: Just one. One egg and a pinch of salt. Not too many extras — keep it simple.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Now the filling. How much meat do you use?

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: 400 grams of minced lamb or beef. Not too little — you need enough filling so the manti aren't empty.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: Two or three large ones. Chop them very finely — they shouldn't have too many big chunks.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: My grandmother adds a little pumpkin — about 150 grams. It adds sweetness. But not too much or it changes the flavour too much.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: How much oil goes into the filling?

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: A few tablespoons. Enough to keep it moist. My advice: don't add too much fat or the manti become greasy.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: How long do you steam them?

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: 35 to 40 minutes. Steam enough so they're cooked through but not too long or the dough goes soft.

questions.text: "How much flour do you need?" — Why "much" not "many"?
questions.hint: "much" = uncountable nouns (flour, water, oil, salt). "many" = countable (eggs, onions, cups).
"many" = countable nouns. You can count onions: one onion, two onions. ✅

questions.text: "Add a ___ pumpkin — about 150 grams." (small amount, uncountable)
questions.hint: "a little" = small amount of uncountable noun. "a little pumpkin" ✅
"too much" = more than what is good or needed. "Too much fat" = an excessive amount.

questions.text: "Steam enough so they're cooked through." "Enough" here means:
questions.hint: "enough" = sufficient, adequate. "Steam enough" = steam for the right amount of time.
"little by little" = gradually, in small amounts. "Add water little by little." ✅

questions.text: "Not too many extras." — "Extras" is countable. What confirms this?
questions.hint: "too many" = used with countable nouns. "Not too many extras" → extras are countable.
"a lot of" = can be used with BOTH countable and uncountable. "a lot of eggs" / "a lot of flour" ✅
